claim: Butterfly wing color patterns play a fundamental role in signaling and crypsis.
source: The patterning and coloration of butterfly wings have been a paradigmatic research focus due to their fundamental role in signaling and crypsis (Beldade and Brakefield, 2002; Sweeney et al., 2003; Tsai et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Significant advances have been made in identifying the cellular and molecular basis of lepidopteran pigmentary coloration.
source: Significant advances have been made recently in identifying the cellular and molecular basis of lepidopteran pigmentary coloration (Matsuoka and Monteiro, 2018; Nadeau et al., 2016; Nishikawa et al., 2015; Reed et al., 2011; Van Belleghem et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2017a).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to recent research

claim: A small number of regulatory genes exert significant influence on pigment synthesis and spatial expression.
source: A small number of regulatory genes have been found to exert significant influence on the synthesis and spatial expression of pigments, as well as regulating cuticle deposition, thereby affecting the overall scale morphology (e.g., Banerjee and Monteiro, 2022; Brien et al., 2022; Ficarrotta et al., 2022; Matsuoka and Monteiro, 2018; Prakash et al., 2022; Van Belleghem et al., 2023; Wee et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Suppression of the optix gene tunes lower lamina thickness and induces iridescent structural coloration.
source: For instance, suppression of the optix gene has been found to tune lower lamina thickness, inducing iridescent structural coloration and affecting cuticular coverage of the upper lamina (Wasik et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citations to specific studies

claim: Recent studies have interrogated the formation of longitudinal ridges in lepidopteran scales.
source: Building on the classic studies on cellular organization of lepidopteran scales (Ghiradella, 1974; Ghiradella, 1985; Ghiradella, 1989; Ghiradella and Radigan, 1976; Overton, 1966), a few recent studies utilized advances in microscopy techniques to interrogate the formation of longitudinal ridges (Day et al., 2019; Dinwiddie et al., 2014; McDougal et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to classic and recent studies

claim: Contemporary research on scale cell development focuses on a few nymphalid model taxa.
source: Moreover, contemporary research on scale cell development focuses on just a few model taxa (Bicyclus, Precis, Heliconius, Vanessa) all from the family of Nymphalidae (Beldade and Brakefield, 2002; Brien et al., 2022; Day et al., 2019; Dinwiddie et al., 2014; Matsuoka and Monteiro, 2018; Nadeau et al., 2016; Pomerantz et al., 2020; Prakash et al., 2022 ; Reed et al., 2011; Sweeney et al., 2003; Van Belleghem et al., 2023; Wasik et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017b)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on nymphalid species

claim: There is overwhelming diversity in the hierarchical organization of scale nanostructures across Lepidoptera.
source: despite an overwhelming diversity in the hierarchical organization of scale nanostructures across Lepidoptera (Ghiradella, 1984; Ghiradella, 1985; Ghiradella, 1989; Prum et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies documenting diversity

claim: Bric à brac acts as a genetic switch that suppresses UV-reflecting Christmas tree-like ridge gratings in male Colias butterflies.
source: A rare exception is the recent work on pierid butterfly Colias identifying bric à brac as a genetic switch that suppresses UV-reflecting Christmas tree-like ridge gratings in males (Ficarrotta et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to a specific study

claim: Understanding scale organization in diverse lepidopterans is relevant to challenges in synthesizing complex hierarchical nanostructures.
source: Deciphering the cellular and developmental basis of scale organization in beyond just a few model lepidopterans is also highly relevant to current challenges in the synthesis of complex sub-micron and micron-scale hierarchical nanostructures, and could inspire novel biomimetic routes to fabricate multifunctional nanomaterials (Kolle et al., 2010; McDougal et al., 2019; Pokroy et al., 2009; Potyrailo et al., 2007; Siddique et al., 2017; Wilts et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on biomimetic applications

claim: The bauplan of lepidopteran wing scales consists of an ornamented upper lamina over a relatively unstructured basal lamina, supported by arches with trabeculae.
source: The bauplan of lepidopteran wing scales consists an ornamented upper lamina over a relatively unstructured basal lamina, supported by arches with pillar-like struts called trabeculae (Ghiradella, 1984; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citation and reference to figure

claim: The upper lamina is comprised of longitudinal ridges with transverse crossribs framing rectilinear windows.
source: The upper lamina is comprised of longitudinal ridges with transverse crossribs framing a set of rectilinear windows.
evidence: Describes established structural features of scales

claim: Scale windows typically open into the interior lumen but can also be covered by a thin cuticular lamina.
source: These windows typically open into the interior lumen of the scale cell, but can also be covered by a thin layer of cuticular lamina (Ghiradella, 1984).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: The sides of ridges feature microribs visible at higher magnifications under electron microscopy.
source: The sides of the ridges feature microribs – fine flute-like stripes visible at higher magnifications under an electron microscope (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to figure showing electron microscopy data

claim: Papilionidae encompasses the known diversity of scale nanostructure and exhibits some of the most complex hierarchical morphologies found in nature.
source: Among all Lepidoptera families, swallowtail butterflies (Papilionidae) not only encompasses the known diversity of scale nanostructure, but also exhibit some of the most complex hierarchical morphologies found in nature (Ghiradella, 1984; Ghiradella, 1985; Ghiradella, 1989; Prum et al., 2006; Saranathan et al., 2010; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to figure

claim: Current research on papilionids is limited to the molecular basis of mimicry of pigment patterns.
source: Despite having a few model species (e.g., Papilio xuthus, Papilio polytes, and Papilio machaon), the focus of the current research on papilionids is limited to the molecular basis of mimicry of pigment patterns (e.g., Nishikawa et al., 2015; Yoda et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on papilionid pigment patterns

claim: Papilionid wing scales exhibit irregular veins or mesh-like crossribs, often with an underlying honeycomb-like lattice of cuticular walls enclosing columnar pores.
source: The wing scales of papilionid species (e.g., Parides sesostris, Papilio nireus) exhibit irregular veins or mesh-like crossribs, often with an underlying honeycomb-like lattice of cuticular walls enclosing columnar pores (Ghiradella, 1984; Ghiradella, 1985; Ghiradella and Radigan, 1976; Prum et al., 2006; Saranathan et al., 2010; Wilts et al., 2014; Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citations and references to figures

claim: Irregular crossribs are an autapomorphy of papilionid butterflies.
source: In any case, these irregular crossribs are an autapomorphy of papilionid butterflies (Ghiradella, 1984; Ghiradella, 1985; Ghiradella and Radigan, 1976)
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on papilionid scale morphology

claim: Irregular crossribs are thought to increase the surface area over which pigments such as papiliochromes can be deposited.
source: that are thought to increase the surface area over which pigments such as papiliochromes can be deposited (Wilts et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to a study on pigment deposition

claim: Irregular crossribs likely play a role in thermoregulation as they are efficient absorbers of solar radiation.
source: and likely play a role in thermoregulation as they are efficient absorbers of solar radiation (Siddique et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study on solar radiation absorption

claim: P. eurimedes adult male has structurally colored green patches on dorsal forewings.
source: (A) Adult male with structurally colored green patches on their dorsal forewings.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1A

source: (B) Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) top view and (C) Focused ion beam (FIB)-SEM cross-sectional image of an adult green scale showing ridges and honeycomb lattice ending in trabeculae on top of a perforated multilayer lattice.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B and C with SEM and FIB-SEM imaging

claim: Early stages of scale cell growth in P. polytes and P. eurimedes are as previously documented in several nymphalid species.
source: Early stages of scale cell growth are as previously documented in several nymphalid species (Day et al., 2019; Dinwiddie et al., 2014; Ghiradella, 1974; Pomerantz et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

source: Alternatively, the crossrib pattern could be produced as a result of spontaneous processes like Ostwald ripening, phase separation, and/or biomechanical forces determined by the mechanical properties of the membranes, leading to stable, quasi-periodic, foam-like perforations on the plasma membrane in between ridges (Dinwiddie et al., 2014; Elson et al., 2010; McDougal et al., 2021; Rosetti et al., 2017; Voorhees, 1985; Wilts et al., 2019).

claim: The presence of chitinous disks followed by F-actin reorganization appears to be specific to species with extended honeycomb lattice walls.
source: Overall, the presence of chitinous disks followed by F-actin reorganization appears to be specific to species with extended honeycomb lattice walls, for example, P. eurimedes, P. arcas, and P. nireus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and E).
evidence: Inference from comparative observations across species

claim: Reorganized actin structures are not observed in species with shallow irregular crossribs, such as P. polytes.
source: Such reorganized actin structures are not observed in species with shallow irregular crossribs, such as P. polytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6

claim: Several Papilio species possess multilayered cover scales with widely spaced and reduced ridges.
source: On the other hand, several Papilio species (e.g., palinurus, blumei, karna) possess multilayered cover scales (Ghiradella, 1974; Prum et al., 2006; Trzeciak et al., 2012) with widely spaced and reduced (in both height and number) ridges.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on these species

claim: Multilayered cover scales in some Papilio species have no apparent crossribs, trabeculae, or honeycombs.
source: These scales have no apparent crossribs, trabeculae, or honeycombs.
evidence: Description of scale morphology

claim: The dimpled appearance of cover scales is templated by reorganization of F-actin bundles into a whorl-like concave network.
